collection.description: Should a villager take it back, or laugh it off?

ask.text:
The {@chief} is having a bad day. (subject.He/She) has had three arguments before breakfast, a roof has fallen in, and the pigs have got into the garden. When (subject) brings (subject.him/her) a bowl of soup, the {@chief} sighs and says, "I'd give anything to be you today. Just carry soup about. No decisions."
(subject) laughs, and says, "And I'd give anything to be {@chief} for a day," without thinking. Over by the fire, the old storyteller, (elder), looks up sharply. (subject.He/She) knows a story about a {@chief} and a villager who said exactly those words to each other, under a full moon, and it is a full moon tonight.
(elder) is staring at them. Should (subject) take it back, or laugh it off?

c1o1.text: In the morning, (subject) wakes up in the {@chief}'s hut, in the {@chief}'s body. The {@chief} wakes up in (subject)'s. The story, it turns out, was true. They try everything to swap back. Nothing works. So the {@chief} goes on being {@chief} from inside (subject)'s body, and (subject) carries soup about in the {@chief}'s. "Be careful what you say under a full moon," says (elder), who is not surprised.

c1o2.text: In the morning, nothing has happened, except that (subject) wakes up wearing a perfect copy of the {@chief}'s clothes, feathers and all. (subject.He/She) didn't own any clothes like that last night. The {@chief} laughs so hard (subject.he/she) has to sit down, and says (subject) can keep them. Nobody can tell where they came from. (elder) says the moon has a sense of humour.

c1.text: "It's only a saying," says (subject), and the {@chief} laughs too, tiredly. (elder) shakes (elder.his/her) head and goes back to the fire, muttering. That night the full moon comes up huge and white over the sea...

c2o1.text: (subject) took it back. The {@chief} didn't. In the morning they are each in the other's body, and the {@chief}, in (subject)'s body, is cheerfully carrying soup round the village, whistling, while (subject), in the {@chief}'s, deals with the pigs. "One day," says the {@chief}. "Just one day." It is longer than one day.

c2o2.text: The moon comes up and nothing happens. But the {@chief} sits with (subject) by the fire long into the night, and talks about how tired (subject.he/she) is. In the morning, (subject) takes half the {@chief}'s small jobs off (subject.his/her) hands without being asked: the pigs, the roof, the arguments about the roof. The {@chief} has a much better day.

c2.text: "I didn't mean it!" says (subject), loudly, to the sky. The {@chief} looks at (subject.him/her) oddly. (elder) nods, satisfied. Then the {@chief} says, very quietly, "I did, though..."
